title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
authors: Elisabeth Fink
abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

infographic.key_insight: GTFormer replaces self-attention with a syntax-free hierarchical graph network, reporting 8192× length extrapolation with linear-time computation and linear memory.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bounded-degree graph processing could make very long code, log, and retrieval workloads practical without quadratic attention costs.
method: Build a balanced binary token hierarchy with ⌈log₂ N⌉ depth.
Add boundary-bridging shift edges and random expander shortcuts.
Combine multi-channel convex highway gating with top-down broadcast.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-perfect accuracy across eight benchmarks when trained only on sequences of length ≤512 and evaluated zero-shot up to 4,194,304 tokens on a single commodity GPU.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify GPU hardware, runtime measurements, or benchmark details needed to assess practical efficiency and generalization.
infographic.paper_title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time

title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization
authors: Shuo Chen, Li Cui, Cunxin Huang, Ya-Feng Liu, Minghang Xie, Meng Xu
abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: NextEval uses an LLM agent to coordinate numerical methods for derivative-free optimization, aiming to find better solutions with fewer costly objective evaluations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce evaluation costs in simulation-based design and experiments where derivatives are unavailable or expensive.
method: An LLM agent selects numerical tools, configures parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget.
A numerical environment computes and evaluates candidate points while preserving shared history and method-specific state across switches.
NextEval Bench compares agent configurations using shared tasks, identical numerical tools, and matched evaluation budgets and information constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better function-evaluation efficiency than state-of-the-art DFO baselines on low-dimensional problems, without specifying effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond low-dimensional problems and the added cost of LLM orchestration remain unclear from the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization

title: Improving Reasoning with Rollout Agreement for Group-Based Policy Optimization
authors: Sohyun Son, Yerim Hong, Jaeyun Park, Mujeen Sung
abstract: Recent methods for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) use rollout diversity to improve reasoning performance or training efficiency. Despite these gains, the extent to which differences among correct-answer rollouts reflect useful alternative reasoning or unresolved errors remains poorly understood. We investigate this question through a blind paired analysis of a model trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), comparing the highest- and lowest-agreement correct-answer traces for the same problem. Across 126 pairs, low-agreement traces have more spurious reasoning than high-agreement traces (35% vs. 22%), including internal inconsistencies and misuse of problem conditions. Based on these findings, we propose RoAR (Rollout-Agreement Reward), which adds reasoning-level agreement to GRPO's rewards for verified-correct rollouts. RoAR computes this signal from existing on-policy rollout groups, requiring no human-written rationales, additional sampling, or separately trained process evaluator. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the 1.5B GRPO-RoAR model reaches 55.5% mean pass@1 under zero-shot evaluation using 7K training examples, exceeding GRPO and GRPO-CARE by 6.0 and 5.5 percentage points. A separate blind audit of 100 problems answered correctly by all four 1.5B models finds spurious rates of 18% for GRPO-RoAR, 32% for GRPO, 27% for GRPO-CARE, and 37% for DRA-GRPO. Our findings identify reasoning validity as an important consideration when using rollout differences to guide learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/ldi-kyunghee/RoAR.

infographic.key_insight: Agreement among correct-answer rollouts can help reward more reliable reasoning, since a correct final answer can still hide spurious steps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RoAR adds a reasoning-quality signal to GRPO using existing rollout groups, without extra sampling, human-written rationales, or a separately trained process evaluator.
method: Blindly compare high- and low-agreement correct-answer traces for the same problem.
Compute reasoning-level agreement within existing on-policy rollout groups.
Add agreement-based rewards for verified-correct rollouts during GRPO training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five math benchmarks, the 1.5B RoAR model achieved 55.5% mean zero-shot pass@1 after training on 7K examples, beating GRPO by 6.0 percentage points; a separate 100-problem blind audit found 18% spurious reasoning versus GRPO's 32%.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement does not guarantee validity, and the reasoning audit was limited to problems answered correctly by all four compared models.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Reasoning with Rollout Agreement for Group-Based Policy Optimization

title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
authors: Bo Yang, Zishuai Zhang, Weihua Li, Qinnan Zhang, Sijia Wen, Hainan Zhang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.

infographic.key_insight: Guided-RLVR uses a lightweight controller to steer sampling toward diverse reasoning paths, countering the narrow exploration that can arise in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve mathematical reasoning and code generation by broadening exploration during reinforcement learning.
method: Augment RLVR with a lightweight controller.
Inject semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution.
Encourage multiple reasoning perspectives to expand exploration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over existing RLVR methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, alongside more diverse reasoning trajectories, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Controller overhead and sensitivity to steering-token selection are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

title: Log-Derivative Trick for Parametric Markov Chains
authors: Arthur Gall, Ichiro Hasuo, Thomas Seiller
abstract: Optimizing expected rewards and reachability probabilities in parametric Markov chains (pMCs) is central to the analysis and synthesis of probabilistic systems with loops. While traditional symbolic synthesis approaches--such as parameter lifting and rational function generation--suffer from scalability bottlenecks, gradient-based optimization emerges as an effective alternative. However, existing gradient-based techniques still rely on symbolic gradient computation--such as solving large linear systems--over the global state space, inheriting scalability limits. Finite-horizon approximation is possible but introduces uncontrollable bias. In this paper, we introduce a scalable Monte Carlo gradient estimator based on a measure-theoretic generalization of the log-derivative trick. We prove that our estimator provides unbiased gradient estimates under almost-sure termination and standard regularity conditions. Crucially, our method avoids global state-space materialization and linear system solving entirely: it operates purely along sampled trajectories, requiring only black-box evaluations of local transition probabilities (or densities) and their derivatives. Unlike existing pMC techniques that are fundamentally restricted to finite discrete systems, our measure-theoretic framework naturally extends to continuous and general $σ$-finite state spaces. Empirical evaluations on synthetic discrete pMCs and continuous-state case studies demonstrate that our method scales to state spaces far beyond the reach of existing solvers, significantly reducing execution time without introducing bias.

infographic.key_insight: A measure-theoretic log-derivative estimator yields unbiased Monte Carlo gradients for parametric Markov chains without constructing the global state space or solving large linear systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables gradient-based optimization of expected rewards and reachability probabilities in large probabilistic systems, including continuous-state models.
method: Sample trajectories using local transition probabilities or densities and their derivatives.
Apply a generalized log-derivative trick to estimate objective gradients.
Establish unbiasedness under almost-sure termination and standard regularity conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations on synthetic discrete chains and continuous-state cases, with lower execution times and scaling beyond existing solvers, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Unbiasedness depends on termination and regularity assumptions; estimator variance and long trajectories may still affect practical efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: Log-Derivative Trick for Parametric Markov Chains

title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization
authors: Don Li
abstract: By virtue of the sheer compute demands of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), modern multi-core microprocessors suffer from severe power density limits and thermal throttling, entailing an urgent need for principled methods for predictive, physics-informed dynamical thermal management (DTM). Here, we introduce a hardware/software co-design physics-informed PDE-constrained DTM throttling optimal control algorithm, ADACT (Adjoint-Driven Adaptive Co-Design Thermal Control), that minimizes thermal risk and cooling energy overhead while maximizing core execution throughput. The underlying physical temperature field is governed by a two-dimensional nonhomogeneous parabolic reaction-diffusion equation with spatially localized, time-varying power source terms and variable convective cooling subject to nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We employ a discretization of the continuous state PDE via a Crank-Nicolson finite difference scheme with a 5-point discrete Laplacian operator on a uniform spatial mesh, which preserves unconditional numerical stability and $O(Δx^2 + Δy^2 + Δt^2)$ second-order temporal and spatial accuracy. To efficiently compute exact gradients, we construct and implement a continuous backward-in-time adjoint state method with L-BFGS as our optimization algorithm of choice. The accuracy and second-order convergence rates of both forward state and backward adjoint solvers are quantitatively verified via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and gradient accuracy is validated using directional derivative Taylor tests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ADACT dynamically throttles software power workloads and modulates hardware cooling efforts to strictly uphold physical thermal thresholds while maintaining operational throughput.

infographic.key_insight: ADACT jointly optimizes workload throttling and cooling using a physics-based thermal PDE to balance temperature risk, cooling energy, and processor throughput.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers predictive thermal management for power-dense AI and HPC processors by coordinating software workloads with hardware cooling.
method: Model chip temperature with a 2D reaction–diffusion PDE, localized power sources, and variable cooling.
Discretize with second-order Crank–Nicolson time stepping and a five-point finite-difference Laplacian.
Use backward adjoint gradients and L-BFGS to optimize workload and cooling controls.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution tests verify second-order state and adjoint convergence, Taylor tests validate gradients, and numerical experiments report thermal-threshold compliance while maintaining throughput.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical validation, not deployment on physical processors; real-world performance depends on thermal-model calibration and control-loop cost.
infographic.paper_title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization

title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning
authors: Ege Gursoy, Nicolas Mansard
abstract: A central limitation of modern machine learning systems is the lack of formal certificates guaranteeing their behavior beyond empirical, sample-based evaluation. Sum-of-squares (SOS) methods provide such guarantees by certifying polynomial inequalities over continuous domains via semidefinite programming (SDP). While prior work has introduced SDP layers as differentiable components in neural networks, repeated learning calls can lose the computational benefit of the forward program's sparse representation. We propose Sparse SOS Layers, differentiable value layers whose backward passes reuse the local coordinates of the forward solve. Under a fixed template and learned objective coefficients, each layer avoids building dense certificates and reuses its sparse structure across training steps. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves up to 2.7 times speedup in total warm-call time, with nearly 100 times lower memory usage (1.7 vs. 160 GiB) for relatively large problem sizes for the tested dense parameterization. Experiments cover sparse polynomial certification, pendulum control, combinatorial relaxations, robotics projection, oscillator chains, and pose graph synchronization. A design study achieves zero certified violations across unseen problem instances and sizes, while requiring roughly 7 times fewer optimization solves than estimating gradients by perturbing the objective coefficients and re-solving the problem (finite differences). These results show that sparse certificate values can be effectively integrated into learning pipelines when the backward pass respects the verifier's structure.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse SOS Layers integrate polynomial inequality certificates into learning while preserving the forward solver’s sparse structure during backpropagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: They make certificate-based learning more practical for control, robotics, and optimization by reducing repeated-solve time and memory use.
method: Represent polynomial certification problems as differentiable SOS value layers.
Reuse the forward solve’s local sparse coordinates in the backward pass.
Keep the problem template fixed while learning objective coefficients, avoiding dense certificate construction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six application areas, tests report up to 2.7× faster total warm-call time and 1.7 versus 160 GiB memory for a tested dense parameterization; a design study reports zero certified violations on unseen instances and sizes with roughly 7× fewer solves than finite differences.
infographic.watch_item: The approach assumes a fixed template with learned objective coefficients; reported gains may not extend to changing constraint structures or other parameterizations.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning

title: Axiomatic Learning and Probabilistic Structures with first applications to variants of Arithmetic Machine Learning and beyond
authors: Vlad Margarint
abstract: We introduce the Axiomatic Learning Structures (ALS) and Axiomatic Probabilistic Structure (APS) in order to study the interactions of Machine Learning, Optimization, with research frameworks- which, we take the view, can be characterized at the core by the corresponding axioms. The ALS explores the interplays between structures that one is interested in Learning Theory such as Loss functions and the axioms of the objects and transformations involved in these functions. The APS studies the interaction between structures of interest in Probability Theory such as Gibbs distributions, equations with noise, etc. and the axioms of the corresponding objects and transformations. We also introduce in Section 6 Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) on Mathematical data-sets. One feature of this approach is the ranking of transformations from a table for a certain task based on scores which reflect which transformations work better than others, similarly to when human investigators try various methods on a task. We also study structure recovery from noisy data. In particular, to exemplify the ideas, we consider loss functions which contain derivations and derivations-like transformations. As a first application we study recovery in the context of polynomials with integer coefficients using standard derivatives along with other types of derivations which appear in Arithmetic: the p-derivations which satisfy \textit{different axioms} from the usual derivatives. As a first application of the APS we study a class of noisy (partial/mixed) derivations equations. In the last sections, to provide further potential applications of this framework, we give an overview of an initial simplified Opinion Dynamics model and its (simultaneous) study of rules of updates.

infographic.key_insight: Axiomatic Learning Structures (ALS) and Axiomatic Probabilistic Structures (APS) connect learning and probability methods to the axioms governing mathematical objects and transformations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support structure-aware recovery from noisy mathematical data and task-specific selection of transformations.
method: Relate loss functions and probabilistic models to the axioms of their underlying objects and transformations.
Use Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) to rank candidate transformations by task-specific scores.
Explore integer-polynomial recovery using standard derivatives and arithmetic p-derivations, alongside noisy derivation equations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes mathematical applications to polynomial recovery and noisy derivation equations, but reports no dataset sizes, benchmark comparisons, or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability and the reliability of transformation-ranking scores remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Axiomatic Learning and Probabilistic Structures with first applications to variants of Arithmetic Machine Learning and beyond

title: Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control via Trajectory Optimization
authors: Emmanuel S. Ameh, Samuel E. Otto
abstract: The curse of dimensionality associated with solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for the value function remains a key obstacle for real-time optimal feedback control of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems. This is especially severe in aerospace applications such as relaminarizing unsteady turbulent flows and recovering from aerodynamic stall where nonlinear dynamics play a significant role. We introduce Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control (BASOC), a model reduction framework which seeks to find directions in state space along which the value function is most sensitive, and the distribution of states exhibits maximum variance along optimal trajectories. BASOC leverages trajectory optimization and the Pontryagin minimum principle to obtain state and co-state (value function gradient) data along locally optimal trajectories for constructing state and gradient covariance matrices. Balancing these matrices provides an oblique projection for approximating the value function, which can also be used to construct reduced-order models and surrogate feedback control laws. We show that for linear-quadratic optimal control problems, BASOC becomes equivalent to a snapshot method for initial condition balancing of the optimally controlled closed-loop realization. The framework is demonstrated on a nonlinear three-dimensional system where POD and balanced truncation are known to perform poorly, and on the nonlinear complex Ginzburg-Landau equation to demonstrate feasibility for larger-scale systems.

infographic.key_insight: BASOC reduces nonlinear optimal-control problems by balancing state variation along locally optimal trajectories with directions of high value-function sensitivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support real-time feedback control of high-dimensional nonlinear systems by enabling reduced-order models and surrogate control laws.
method: Use trajectory optimization and Pontryagin’s minimum principle to collect state and co-state data.
Construct and balance state and value-gradient covariance matrices.
Use the resulting oblique projection to approximate the value function in reduced coordinates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on a nonlinear three-dimensional system and the nonlinear complex Ginzburg–Landau equation, plus equivalence to closed-loop initial-condition balancing in the linear-quadratic case.
infographic.watch_item: Reliance on locally optimal trajectory data may limit accuracy outside the sampled state regions.
infographic.paper_title: Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control via Trajectory Optimization

title: The Geometry of Manifold Learning: Singular foliations via Deep Learning models
authors: Gabriele Novelli, Eliot Tron, Emanuele Latini, Rita Fioresi
abstract: Deep learning algorithms have become widely used and successful across a wide range of tasks. A key challenge is determining whether these algorithms truly capture the intrinsic geometry of their training data in order to better understand what they learn from data. In this theoretical work, we explore a new geometric structure defined on the data space by a trained neural network through the Data Information Matrix (DIM), a variation of the Fisher Information Matrix. This new geometric structure is a foliation and the main focus of this work is to explore the non-smooth case of ReLU activation functions, where traditional geometric tools often fail. The foliation is defined through a distribution spanned by the columns of the DIM. We first prove that this distribution is non-smooth in the sense of distributions, rendering the existence of an associated foliation much more complex. To circumvent this issue, we introduce a smoothed version of this distribution that differs from the original only on a set of measure zero. Finally, we prove that this smoothed distribution induces a singular foliation on the data space, which is based on the data the network has been trained with. Our theoretical contributions provide a geometric framework to better understand how neural networks organize their input space in non-smooth settings, bridging differential geometry and deep learning theory.

infographic.key_insight: A trained ReLU network defines a non-smooth geometric distribution through its Data Information Matrix, and a modified version induces a singular foliation of input space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework could help engineers analyze how trained neural networks organize input space, without establishing practical performance gains.
method: Form a distribution from the columns of the Data Information Matrix.
Prove its non-smoothness and introduce a smoothed version differing only on a measure-zero set.
Prove that the modified distribution induces a singular foliation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical proofs, with no datasets, empirical evaluations, or quantitative benchmarks described.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement outside a measure-zero set does not by itself establish numerical stability or practical computability near non-smooth boundaries.
infographic.paper_title: The Geometry of Manifold Learning: Singular foliations via Deep Learning models

title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities
authors: Mateo Díaz, Nicolás García Trillos, Daniel López-Castaño, Congwei Yang
abstract: Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: Wasserstein approximation by measures supported on orthogonal axes identifies a basis for sparse data representation, with near-parametric frame recovery under mild assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a principled way to select sparse coordinate systems within learned subspaces for unsupervised representation learning.
method: Approximate the data distribution with measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame.
Optimize a nonsmooth objective over the orthogonal group O(d).
Use a coarsely Lipschitz bound to analyze empirical minimizers and locally initialized stochastic gradient optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a recovery rate of Õ_d(n^−1/2) and numerical experiments supporting the theory, but provides no dataset or benchmark details.
infographic.watch_item: The stochastic gradient guarantee requires local initialization, and the stated rate can hide dimension-dependent factors.
infographic.paper_title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities

title: An Algebra of Transformers
authors: Yong Wang, Zhiyan Wang, Hexiao Kang
abstract: On the theoretic analyses on transforms, they mainly focus on the computability analysis, such the Turing-completeness of unbounded precision transformers, the advantage of parallelizability of unbounded precision transformers and the limitations of bounded precision transformers. This paper give transformers an algebra for reasoning, which relies heavily on the functional decomposition results of transformers. This algebra uses functional decompositions as atomic actions, includes sequential composition and parallel composition, recursion for feedback and abstraction for hidden layers. As we know, it is the first attempt to model transformers logically and can be used to verify the correctness of transformer based applications.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes an algebra for reasoning about transformers, treating functional decompositions as atomic actions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework could support formal correctness verification of transformer-based applications.
method: Use transformer functional decompositions as atomic actions.
Combine actions through sequential and parallel composition.
Represent feedback with recursion and hidden layers with abstraction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical framework but reports no datasets, empirical evaluations, or verification case studies.
infographic.watch_item: Practical verification depends on obtaining suitable functional decompositions; the abstract does not establish scalability to deployed transformers.
infographic.paper_title: An Algebra of Transformers

title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models
authors: Edric Tam, Qingyang Liu, Barbara Engelhardt, Ray Bai
abstract: Broad classes of deep generative models (DGMs) operate by learning to map a simple source distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, to a complex high-dimensional target distribution. Despite their success, DGMs often empirically struggle to accurately represent distributions with heavy tails or well-separated modes. In this work, we show that these difficulties reflect intrinsic properties of the underlying transport problem rather than particular neural network architectures or training procedures. We establish quantitative lower bounds on the gradients and Jacobians of pushforward mappings that transport log-concave source distributions to such targets. For heavy-tailed target distributions, the required gradient magnitude grows as the target develops increasingly large moments. For multimodal target distributions, the low-probability regions between well-separated modes similarly force large gradients in the transport map. We discuss how such large derivatives relate to trade-offs between expressivity and numerical stability. Our results hold under substantially weaker regularity conditions than previous analyses and remain stable under perturbations of the target distribution. Finally, we show that these obstructions can be mitigated when the goal is approximation of a given density rather than generative modeling. Specifically, we propose simple classes of bijective reparametrizations that can alleviate the difficult geometric structure and reduce the gradient burden placed on the learned generative map. Numerical experiments support our theoretical analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Transporting a log-concave source to heavy-tailed or well-separated multimodal targets intrinsically requires large gradients, regardless of the generative model architecture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These gradient barriers expose an expressivity–numerical stability trade-off when designing pushforward deep generative models.
method: Derive quantitative gradient and Jacobian lower bounds for heavy-tailed and multimodal targets.
Establish results under weaker regularity assumptions and target perturbations.
Propose bijective reparametrizations to reduce gradient burdens in density approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis, but the abstract provides no datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The reparametrization mitigation applies to density approximation and should not be assumed to remove barriers in generative sampling.
infographic.paper_title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models

title: Constraint Learning by Optimizing over Trained Neural Networks: A Pragmatic Tutorial
authors: Jiaxiao Fang, Thiago Serra
abstract: Constraint learning is an emerging paradigm of modeling optimization problems with the help of machine learning. In this paradigm, trained machine learning models are embedded into the optimization model. For example, we can learn constraints empirically from available data, or we can avoid using a nonlinear objective function by learning a simpler approximation for it. Neural networks become a compelling option if the machine learning models must capture more elaborate and nuanced relationships. However, optimization models embedding neural networks may become too large or too slow to solve. In this tutorial, we present practical considerations for an effective and efficient use of constraint learning with neural networks and validate it with a case study highlighting the benefit of smaller and sparser networks.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding trained neural networks into optimization models enables data-driven constraints and objective approximations, but smaller, sparser networks can make these models more practical to solve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can incorporate empirically learned relationships into optimization while managing the computational cost of neural-network representations.
method: Train neural networks to represent constraints or approximate nonlinear objectives.
Embed the trained networks into optimization models.
Consider network size and sparsity to improve computational tractability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a case study highlighting the benefit of smaller and sparser networks, without specifying datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Embedded neural networks may make optimization models too large or slow to solve, so predictive fit must be weighed against computational tractability.
infographic.paper_title: Constraint Learning by Optimizing over Trained Neural Networks: A Pragmatic Tutorial

title: Understanding Practical Optimization in Machine Learning
authors: Egor Shulgin
abstract: Modern machine learning relies on practical optimization methods that often differ from the algorithms studied in classical analyses: they train submodels, clip or normalize gradients, use layer-wise non-Euclidean directions, or approximate costly inner computations. This thesis analyzes the objective, assumptions, update, and computation defined by these procedures, rather than those of simplified proxies. For submodel training, we show that Independent Subnetwork Training can converge to a shifted fixed point because sketching before differentiation biases the update for the original objective. Model-Agnostic Sparsified Training instead incorporates the sketch distribution into its objective, which makes sketched gradients unbiased and admits convergence guarantees. For private optimization, we show that adaptive quantile clipping retains bias at any fixed quantile, while suitable quantile schedules recover near-optimal nonconvex rates under heavy-tailed noise. We then combine smoothed normalization with error compensation and obtain distributed private convergence guarantees under standard assumptions, without assuming bounded gradients. For optimizers based on linear minimization oracles, we develop and validate a layer-wise generalized smoothness model and build on it the Gluon framework for Muon- and Scion-style methods. We also show that the approximate orthogonalization in Muon matters: less precise orthogonalization calls for smaller stepsizes, so its precision should be tuned together with the learning rate. Overall, practical methods are better understood when theory retains the features that determine their optimization behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Optimization theory better explains practical machine learning when it preserves algorithmic features such as sketching, clipping, normalization, and approximate orthogonalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training reliability depends on matching objectives, clipping schedules, and learning rates to the actual update rules and numerical approximations.
method: Analyze submodel objectives to distinguish biased Independent Subnetwork Training from unbiased Model-Agnostic Sparsified Training.
Study quantile clipping schedules and combine smoothed normalization with error compensation for distributed private optimization.
Develop layer-wise generalized smoothness and the Gluon framework for Muon- and Scion-style methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence guarantees, near-optimal nonconvex rates under heavy-tailed noise, and validation of a layer-wise smoothness model, but gives no datasets or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: In Muon, less precise approximate orthogonalization requires smaller stepsizes, so precision and learning rate should be tuned together.
infographic.paper_title: Understanding Practical Optimization in Machine Learning

title: Lie Symmetry-Guided Adaptive Sampling for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Runze Zhao
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), with broad applications in physics, engineering, and medicine. However, their performance is highly sensitive to the sampling strategy for training points. Conventional uniform sampling often fails to adequately resolve regions with complex solution features, leading to low efficiency and limited accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose a Lie symmetry-driven adaptive sampling framework for PINNs, termed Lie-AS-ISC. For PDEs admitting Lie symmetry groups, symmetry transformations are exploited to derive intrinsic functional relationships between the solution and its variables, enabling the construction of basis points with exact solutions that span the solution domain. Building on this, an adaptive sampling strategy is developed by jointly considering absolute error and invariant surface conditions, while a dual-index loss is introduced to enhance training constraints. The proposed method significantly improves prediction accuracy. The experimental results show that this method consistently outperforms existing methods in accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Lie-AS-ISC uses PDE Lie symmetries to guide adaptive sampling and improve physics-informed neural network accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could improve mesh-free PDE solvers in engineering by targeting training points beyond conventional uniform sampling.
method: Use Lie symmetry transformations to derive solution–variable relationships and construct basis points with exact solutions.
Adapt sampling using both absolute error and invariant surface conditions.
Introduce a dual-index loss to strengthen training constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistently higher accuracy than existing methods in experiments, but provides no benchmarks, numerical gains, or computational costs.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability depends on identifying usable PDE Lie symmetries and constructing the required exact-solution basis points.
infographic.paper_title: Lie Symmetry-Guided Adaptive Sampling for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: Automatic Certified Differentiation in Lean
authors: Ramy Shahin
abstract: Automatic differentiation (the automatic computation of numerical function derivatives) has many applications, especially in scientific computing and machine learning. Several approaches to automate the calculation of derivatives have been presented. Common challenges facing those approaches include (1) having to define derivative rules for different classes of functions, (2) having to manipulate program symbols to understand the semantics of the function being differentiated, and construct the derivative function, and (3), more importantly, ensuring that the calculated derivative is correct. In this paper, we present an approach for automatic \emph{certified} differentiation using the Lean proof assistant. By certified, we mean a correctness certificate is computed together with the derivative function and a domain on which the derivative is guaranteed to be valid. Our approach leverages existing derivative theorems included in the Mathlib Lean library instead of having to define our own rules. We also utilize Lean metaprogramming to manipulate the symbolic structure of the input function, and to construct the derivative function. The correctness certificate is computed step-wise as we apply Mathlib theorems. To make the search efficient, we index the derivative theorems by the function they differentiate. We evaluate our approach on 500 randomly generated functions: with the index, all of them are differentiated, with a median time of 0.18\,s per function, 8.6 times faster than without the index.

infographic.key_insight: Lean can automatically construct a derivative, a correctness certificate, and a domain on which the derivative is guaranteed valid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certified differentiation can support scientific computing and machine learning workflows that require formally verified derivative calculations.
method: Reuse derivative theorems from Lean’s Mathlib library.
Use Lean metaprogramming to construct derivatives and correctness certificates step by step.
Index derivative theorems by the functions they differentiate to accelerate search.
infographic.evidence_signal: With theorem indexing, all 500 randomly generated test functions were differentiated, with a median time of 0.18 seconds per function—8.6× faster than without indexing.
infographic.watch_item: Success on randomly generated functions does not establish coverage or performance for large, real-world computational models.
infographic.paper_title: Automatic Certified Differentiation in Lean

title: Boundary Geometry Determines Optimal Shallow ReLU Approximation under Weighted Coefficient Constraints
authors: Jia-Qi Yang, Lei Shi
abstract: We study how boundary geometry affects $L^q$ approximation by shallow ReLU neural networks on convex bodies $K\subset\mathbb R^d$. The target classes are unit balls of weighted variation spaces that can enlarge classical spaces by incorporating domain geometry into constraints on output coefficients. We establish upper and lower bounds for arbitrary convex bodies and determine the optimal polynomial approximation exponents for all planar convex bodies and their products with polytopes, including cubes and circular cylinders. For $C^2$ convex bodies, we determine the optimal exponents in a dimension-dependent range of $q$ extending beyond $2$. When all principal curvatures are positive, the result extends to every finite $q\ge2$. For these classes, the dependence of the optimal exponent on the domain is captured by a single geometric growth exponent associated with small boundary caps. We also identify sharp weight thresholds for retaining the classical approximation exponent and improve previous weights on Euclidean balls while preserving the classical $L^2$ approximation rate. When the target is given as a finite ReLU network, the upper bounds can be realized by a compressed network using only the original neurons, without increasing the weighted coefficient sum. These results show that boundary geometry can change the optimal exponent even when dimension, error norm, and weighting rule are fixed.

infographic.key_insight: Boundary geometry can change the optimal shallow ReLU approximation exponent even when dimension, error norm, and coefficient-weighting rule remain fixed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For finite ReLU targets, the bounds yield compressed networks using only original neurons without increasing the weighted coefficient sum.
method: Incorporate domain geometry into weighted variation-space constraints.
Prove approximation upper and lower bounds using boundary-cap growth.
Identify optimal exponents and sharp weight thresholds for specified convex domains.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds and optimality results for all planar convex bodies, their products with polytopes, and specified smooth convex bodies, rather than empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Optimality guarantees depend on domain regularity and the error-norm range; coverage of every finite q ≥ 2 requires positive principal curvatures in the smooth-body results.
infographic.paper_title: Boundary Geometry Determines Optimal Shallow ReLU Approximation under Weighted Coefficient Constraints

title: QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG
authors: Yifan Zhao, Qianyang Zhao, Xinyu Guan, kai wei, Yuming Deng
abstract: Chunking is a fundamental preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet most existing chunkers rely primarily on heuristics. We introduce the Question--Evidence-Supervised Chunker (QESChunker), to our knowledge the first method for constructing static chunk indices from question--evidence supervision. QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. These results recast chunking as supervised, budget-aware index construction for evidence retrieval.

infographic.key_insight: QESChunker unifies overlapping and non-overlapping RAG chunking under a question–evidence utility objective for supervised, budget-aware index construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a principled alternative to heuristic chunking for improving complete-evidence retrieval with a fixed retriever.
method: Build document-specific static indices using human-annotated or LLM-generated question–evidence pairs, without held-out test queries.
Optimize non-overlapping chunks exactly in polynomial time using dynamic programming.
Optimize overlapping chunks with a greedy algorithm offering a (1−1/√e) approximation guarantee for the monotone submodular objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunkers in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings under matched overlap regimes and a fixed hybrid retriever.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires question–evidence supervision; annotation cost and LLM-generated evidence quality warrant validation.
infographic.paper_title: QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG

title: Periodic Solutions and Exponential Attractivity in Hopfield-Type Neural Networks with Generalized Piecewise Constant Arguments: Impulsive and Nonimpulsive Cases
authors: Ricardo Torres Naranjo, Samuel Castillo Apolonio
abstract: We investigate an impulsive Hopfield-type neural network with a generalized piecewise constant argument, including the nonimpulsive case in which all jump terms vanish. The piecewise constant argument is given by $γ(t)=ζ_k$ on each interval $[t_k,t_{k+1})$, where $t_k\leqζ_k\leq t_{k+1}$, $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$. Depending on the position of $ζ_k$, the argument may be advanced, retarded, or of mixed type. By representing periodic solutions through a Green function and applying a fixed-point argument, we obtain explicit and verifiable sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of an $ω$-periodic solution. We then use a Gronwall-type estimate, together with period averages, to prove that this solution is globally exponentially attractive. These conditions can be checked directly from the system parameters, without requiring explicit knowledge of the periodic solution. In the course of the analysis, we also revisit and correct some estimates presented by Pinto et al. \cite{Pinto_ejqtde}. The case $ζ_k=t_k$ reduces to their setting, whereas our results cover the more general choice of $ζ_k$ within each interval. We also present examples illustrating different types of piecewise constant arguments.

infographic.key_insight: Explicit, parameter-checkable sufficient conditions guarantee a unique periodic solution and global exponential attraction in impulsive and nonimpulsive Hopfield-type networks with generalized piecewise constant arguments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results support analysis of periodic operating regimes in neural dynamical systems with discrete jumps and advanced, retarded, or mixed-type arguments.
method: Represent periodic solutions using a Green function and apply a fixed-point argument.
Combine a Gronwall-type estimate with period averages to establish global exponential attraction.
Extend earlier results to generalized argument placements and correct prior estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mathematical guarantees and illustrative examples of different argument types, rather than empirical benchmark evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees are sufficient, not necessary, and advanced arguments may require special care in numerical simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Periodic Solutions and Exponential Attractivity in Hopfield-Type Neural Networks with Generalized Piecewise Constant Arguments: Impulsive and Nonimpulsive Cases
